title: The Crow and the Snake
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A hungry Crow spied a Snake lying asleep in a sunny spot, and, picking it up in his claws, he was carrying it off to a place where he could make a meal of it without being disturbed, when the Snake reared its head and bit him. It was a poisonous Snake, and the bite was fatal, and the dying Crow said, "What a cruel fate is mine! I thought I had made a lucky find, and it has cost me my life!"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, in what condition did the Crow find the Snake?
options: Lying asleep in a sunny spot
Hiding under a rock
Swimming in a stream
Coiled around a tree branch

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why was the Crow carrying the Snake off to another place?
options: To show it to other crows
To make a meal of it without being disturbed
To drop it into a river
To warn it of danger nearby

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Snake do while being carried off?
options: It fell asleep again
It slipped out of the Crow's claws
It reared its head and bit the Crow
It hissed loudly for help

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what kind of snake had the Crow picked up?
options: A harmless garden snake
A poisonous snake
A very young snake
A snake belonging to a farmer

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what exact words does the dying Crow say?
options: "I should have known better than to trust a snake"
"What a cruel fate is mine! I thought I had made a lucky find, and it has cost me my life!"
"Help me, someone, before it is too late!"
"This snake will pay for what it has done!"

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "fatal" mean in "the bite was fatal"?
options: Painful but temporary
Barely noticeable
Causing death
Easily cured

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Crow call the Snake a "lucky find" before it kills him?
options: He assumed a sleeping snake would make an easy, safe meal
He had been searching for a snake all day
He mistook the snake for a piece of treasure
He wanted to keep the snake as a pet

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Snakes are always more dangerous than they appear at first
Crows should never eat animals they find sleeping
An apparent stroke of good fortune can turn out to carry a fatal, hidden risk
Hunger makes creatures careless about their own safety

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the Crow's condition at the start of the passage?
options: He was hungry
He was injured
He was tired
He was frightened

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the Crow pick up the Snake?
options: In his claws
In his beak
By pushing it with a stick
By trapping it in a net

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Crow say has cost him his life?
options: Chasing a rival crow
What he thought was a lucky find
A fall from a high branch
A fight with another bird

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "reared" mean in "the Snake reared its head"?
options: Lowered gently
Raised up suddenly
Turned away
Shook rapidly

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what mistake did the Crow make in judging the Snake?
options: He assumed a sleeping creature posed no danger to him
He thought the Snake was already dead
He believed the Snake belonged to another crow
He thought the Snake was too small to bite him

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Crow escapes a Snake's bite by flying away in time
A Crow tries to eat a sleeping Snake but is fatally bitten instead
A Snake tricks a Crow into freeing it from a trap
A Crow and a Snake share a meal together peacefully
